function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
Below you’ll find a **complete “recipe”** – from pulling down the repo to committing & pushing your new artefacts back up again.  
I’ve split everything into four logical blocks so you can copy‑paste straight into your terminal (or adapt it to whatever CI/CD pipeline you’re already running).

> ⚠️ **Important:**  
> *These instructions presume you have SSH keys set up for `git@github.com`. If not, replace the SSH URL with HTTPS (`https://github.com/...`) and supply credentials.*  

---

## 0️⃣ Prerequisites

| Tool | Minimum Version |
|------|----------------|
| `git` | ≥ 2.20 |
| `docker` | ≥ 19.03 |
| `kubectl` | ≥ 1.18 |
| `yq` *(optional)* | ≥ 4.0 |

Make sure you’re logged into Docker Hub (or another registry) before building images later.

```bash
# Example login
docker login
```

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the Repository

```bash
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

If you prefer HTTPS:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse the Repo & Generate Artefacts

### 2.1 Inspect What’s Inside

Run a quick scan to understand the project layout:

```bash
tree .
```

Typical output for a minimal Node.js welcome app looks like:

```
├── src/
│   └─ index.js          # entry point
├── package.json         # dependencies & scripts
└── README.md
```

*Key points for our Docker/K8s setup*

| File | Why it matters |
|------|---------------|
| `package.json` | Contains runtime deps (`express`, …) |
| `src/index.js` | Exposes HTTP endpoint on `process.env.PORT || 3000` |
| `.env.example` | Optional env vars (e.g., DB creds) |

Assuming the app listens on `PORT=8080` inside the container (common convention), we’ll tailor the artifacts around that.

---

### 2.2 Create / Update the Dockerfile

#### Manual Approach

Create `/Dockerfile` at the repo root:

```dockerfile
# Stage 1 – Build
FROM node:16-alpine AS builder
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --only=production
COPY ./src ./src
EXPOSE 8080
CMD ["npm","start"]
```

Explanation:

| Step | Purpose |
|-----|---------|
| `node:16-alpine` | Smallest official Node LTS image |
| `npm ci --only=production` | Installs only production deps |
| `EXPOSE 8080` | Declares listening port |
| `CMD ["npm","start"]` | Uses script defined in `package.json` |

> 💡 If you’d rather keep the image tiny, consider multi‑stage builds that strip out dev tooling entirely.

#### Automated Generation via Provided Function

If you’re running this in an environment that supports the helper API, just invoke:

```javascript
const {create_a_docker_file}=require('functions');
await create_a_docker_file({
    directory_name:"./",
    base_image:"node:16-alpine",
    maintainers:"Your Name <you@example.com>",
    expose_port:8080,
    entrypoint:'["npm","start"]'
});
```

*(This writes the same Dockerfile shown above.)*

---

### 2.3 Generate Kubernetes YAML Files

A single manifest containing both Deployment & Service keeps things tidy.

#### Manual Manifest (`k8s/deploy.yaml`)

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: ghcr.io/<your-org>/nodejs-welcome:latest   # <-- update after publishing
        ports:
        - containerPort: 8080
        resources:
          limits:
            cpu: "200m"
            memory: "256Mi"

---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  type: LoadBalancer           # change to ClusterIP / NodePort if needed
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80                   # exposed externally
    targetPort: 8080           # matches containerPort
```

> 🔧 **Tip:** Replace `<your-org>` with your Docker Registry org/user once you publish the image.

#### Automated Creation via Helper

```javascript
const {create_kubernetes_yaml_file}=require('functions');

await create_kubernetes_yaml_file({
    directory_name:"./k8s",
    deployment_name:"nodejs-welcome",
    image_name:"ghcr.io/<your-org>/nodejs-welcome:latest",
    replicas:3,
    port:8080,
    service_type:"LoadBalancer"
});
```

(The helper creates exactly the manifest above.)

---

### 2.4 Set Up GitHub Actions Workflow

Add a workflow under `.github/workflows/docker-build-and-publish.yml`.

```yaml
name: Build & Publish Docker Image

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build_and_publish:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    permissions:
      packages: write     # Needed for GHCR/GitHub Packages
      id-token: write    # Required for OIDC auth (if you choose)
    
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      
      - name: Setup QEMU
        uses: docker/setup-qemu-action@v3
        
      - name: Setup Docker Buildx
        uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3
        
      - name: Log in to GitHub Container Registry
        uses: docker/login-action@v3
        with:
          registry: ghcr.io
          username: ${{ github.actor }}
          password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

      - name: Cache NPM modules
        uses: actions/cache@v4
        with:
          key: ${{ runner.os }}-build-${{ hashFiles('**/package-lock.json') }}
          restore-keys: |
            ${{ runner.os }}-build-
      
      - name: Build and Push Docker image
        uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
        with:
          context: .
          tags: ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }}
          cache-from: type=registry,ref=ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:cache
          cache-to: type=inline
          load: false
          push: true
          
      - name: Clean up old caches
        run: echo "No cleanup required – inline caching handles it."
```

**What this does**

| Step | Description |
|------|-------------|
| Checkout | Pull latest source |
| QEMU / BuildX | Enables cross‑platform builds |
| Login | Authenticates against GHCR |
| Cache | Reuses `node_modules` between jobs |
| Build & Push | Builds image tagged with SHA, pushes to GHCR |
| Inline Caching | Keeps build fast without separate layers |

> 📌 **Remember** to enable *Container Registry* permission for the repo settings → *Actions > General* → *Workflow permissions* → *Read and Write*.

---

## 3️⃣ Stage All New Artifacts

Back in the repo root:

```bash
git add Dockerfile k8s/deploy.yaml .github/workflows/docker-build-and-publish.yml
```

(Feel free to include other supporting docs such as `README.md` updates.)

---

## 4️⃣ Commit & Push Changes

```bash
git commit -m "CI/CD: Added Dockerfile, K8s manifests, and GitHub Actions workflow"
git push origin main
```

Once pushed, the GitHub Actions workflow will trigger automatically, building & publishing the Docker image to GHCR. You can verify the image appears under **Packages** → **Containers** in the repo UI.

Afterwards, apply the Kubernetes config to your cluster:

```bash
kubectl apply -f k8s/deploy.yaml
```

Check pod status:

```bash
kubectl get pods -l app=nodejs-welcome
```

And test the service (assuming LB IP):

```bash
curl http://<load-balancer-ip>
```

--- 

### 🎉 Done!

You now have:

- A lightweight Docker image ready for production.
- Declarative Kubernetes objects for easy scaling.
- An automated CI pipeline that rebuilds whenever you push to `main`.

Happy coding!
